narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is a costly oath kept, and the type (102) is volition — not a feeling that seizes the interior but a stance it takes and holds. No source (103, absent) is named: the passage does not trace where this fidelity comes from, so the reading rests on the act itself, not on its origin. No seat (104, value 'none') is given — this is telling: the operation is not lodged in a named organ (not heart, not tongue); it is a whole-person disposition rather than an interior faculty firing. The bearer (105) is the righteous, the one who may sojourn in God's tent (vv.1–2), inferred from the qualifying clauses that define him. The operation (106) is the event itself: 'he swears to his own hurt and does not change' — integrity that holds even when keeping the word costs him. The target (107) is costly-fidelity: what the interior aims at is not advantage but the standing of its own given word. Manner (108, value 'none') is not specified — no adverb of how (not reluctantly, not gladly); the text reports only that it holds, leaving the inner tone unrecorded. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: the passage does not grade the strength of the resolve, does not narrow it further, and does not name a downstream result within this interior — though the psalm's frame ('shall never be moved', v.5) supplies a corporate reward, no per-item effect is coded here. The coupling (112) is 'swear-to-own-hurt': the swearing is welded to loss; the promise and its cost are held together as one movement, not two. Prohibition (113) is absent — this is framed positively, as a thing done, not a thing forbidden. The discovery note (114) confirms the finding: the interior will not renege on a promise merely because it turned out expensive. The role (115) is characteristic — a genuine trait of the inner life, not a passing qualifier. The locus (116) is internal:ib-state: this is a condition of the inner being, God and neighbour standing as the arena the fidelity acts toward (the oath is sworn before them and to them), while the operation itself is interior.
narratives.story: This is about a person who gives their word and keeps it even when keeping it hurts. The psalm is asking who is fit to be God's guest, and one mark of that person is this: they make a promise, discover it will cost them, and still refuse to back out. It isn't a mood that comes over them; it's a settled choice they hold to. Notice what the text does not say — it never tells us the promise was kept gladly or grudgingly, only that it was kept. The promise and the loss are bound together as a single act, and the point is simply this: the inside of such a person will not break a word just because it became expensive.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'set the LORD always before me', and the type (102) is volition — a chosen act of the will, not an involuntary state. No source (103, absent) is coded: the psalm does not say what prompted the setting, so the reading stands on the practice itself. No seat (104, value 'none'): the setting is not assigned to a bodily organ — significant, because vv.7 and 9 do name the heart ('my heart instructs me', 'my heart is glad'), yet this particular operation is left un-seated, marking it as a whole-self orientation rather than a heart-event. The bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred), the 'I' of the poem. The operation (106) is a sustained practice of attention: the self keeps the LORD continually before it, so that with him at its right hand it will not be shaken. The target (107) is 'God-before-me' — the aim is God held constantly in view. Manner (108, value 'none') is unspecified: the text does not describe the style of the attending. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent — no grading, no narrowing, and no separately coded result, though the passage's own logic ('I shall not be shaken', v.8) shows the steadiness that follows. The coupling (112) is 'set-the-LORD': the act of setting is bound to its object; the steadiness is not an independent achievement but the fruit of the fixed gaze. Prohibition (113) is absent — this is a positive practice. The discovery note (114) states it exactly: this is a chosen, continual orientation, and the steadiness follows from the practice. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state — an interior posture, with God as the arena toward which the whole inner life is turned.
narratives.story: Here a person deliberately keeps God in view all the time — not as a passing thought but as a steady, chosen focus. Because he keeps looking that way, he feels that God stands right beside him, and so he is not thrown off balance by whatever comes. What is striking is that his steadiness isn't a separate strength he works up; it is simply the result of where he keeps looking. The psalm names his glad heart elsewhere, but this particular act belongs to the whole person, not to one part of him. It is a habit of attention, freely chosen and held moment by moment.
narratives.variation_note: The item 'set' has two readings. Here (16:8) the target is God himself held before the inner eye, the locus is internal:ib-state, and the coupling is the resulting steadiness ('shall not be shaken'). At 119:30 the same verb sets God's rules (his word) before the self, with an external:god locus and a covenant-arc coupling. The difference is the object of the setting: a Person to be gazed on versus a rule to be lived by — the same volitional act aimed once at God and once at his law.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'those who keep his covenant', and the type (102) is volition — covenant-keeping as a stance the will maintains. No source (103, absent): the passage does not name what generates the keeping. No seat (104, value 'none'): the keeping is not organ-located; it is the disposition of a whole person, not a faculty. The bearer (105) is the covenant-keepers (inferred), those of v.10. The operation (106) is the event of v.10: all God's paths are steadfast love and faithfulness for those who keep his covenant — fidelity that walks in love; the keeping is the condition under which the whole of God's dealing is experienced as mercy. The target (107) is covenant-fidelity — the aim is holding to God's terms. Manner (108, value 'none'): the style of the keeping is unstated. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent — no grade, no narrowing, no separately-coded result, though the discovery draws out that such a one finds all God's ways to be love. The coupling (112) is 'keep-covenant': the keeping is welded to its object, the covenant and testimonies together. Prohibition (113) is absent — positively framed. The discovery note (114): the interior that holds to God's terms finds all his ways to be love. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state — an interior fidelity, with God as the arena; note the contrast with most other 'keep' readings whose locus is external:god, marking this one as read from the side of the keeper's inner condition rather than from the object kept.
narratives.story: This describes the person who holds to God's agreement with them — who stays true to the terms. The psalm makes a quiet promise to such a person: everything God does toward them will turn out to be love and faithfulness. In other words, the one who keeps faith discovers that every path God leads them down is kindness. The keeping isn't tied to any single part of them; it is simply how they live. And the text does not measure how hard they keep or what reward follows — it only says that fidelity opens the eyes to see that all of God's ways are mercy.
narratives.variation_note: 'keep' (natsar/shamar) has four distinct readings. This one (25:10) reads the keeping from inside the keeper (locus internal:ib-state) as the condition for experiencing God's paths as love; type volition. It differs from 34:13 (keeping the tongue from evil — a speech-restraint), from 78:7 (children keeping commandments as the fruit of hope), and from the 119:2 arc (guarding the testimonies as the mark of the blessed). The shift is in what is kept and to what end: a whole covenant embraced inwardly here, a mouth policed there, a rule obeyed as fruit elsewhere.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep your tongue from evil', and the type (102) is volition — a commanded act of self-restraint the will must perform. No source (103, absent): no origin for the restraint is coded. No seat (104, value 'none'): although the operation concerns the tongue and lips, the keeping itself is not assigned an interior seat — the mouth is the thing governed, not the place from which the governing issues; the reading leaves the governing power un-located, a whole-self act. The bearer (105) is the hearer (inferred), the 'children' addressed in v.11 who desire life (v.12). The operation (106) is the teaching event of v.13: keep the tongue from evil and the lips from deceit — the guarded mouth as the path to life. The target (107) is tongue-guarding — the aim is a mouth kept clean of evil and deceit. Manner (108, value 'none'): the how is unstated. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent — no grade, no narrowing, no separately coded result, though the frame promises 'life' and 'good days' (v.12) as the horizon. The coupling (112) is 'keep-tongue': the keeping is bound to its object, the tongue. Prohibition (113) is absent as a coded row, yet notably the operation is itself negatively shaped ('from evil', 'from deceit') — the guarding is a holding-back; the absence of a prohibition row alongside a restraint-operation shows the restraint is read as a positive discipline, not a rule imposed. The discovery note (114): the interior that wants good life must first police its speech. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state — the disposition is interior, its arena the neighbour who would be harmed by evil or deceitful speech.
narratives.story: The teacher turns to those who want a good and long life and gives them the first step: guard your mouth. Keep your tongue away from evil and your lips from lies. The point is that the desire for a good life has to begin with controlling what you say. The mouth is what gets policed, but the power to police it belongs to the whole person, not to any one part. The psalm doesn't spell out how hard this is or exactly what reward follows — it simply sets a clean tongue as the doorway to the life you are hoping for.
narratives.variation_note: Among the four 'keep' readings, this one (34:13) is the only one whose object is the tongue rather than the covenant or testimonies: keeping here is speech-restraint aimed at the neighbour, the guarded mouth as the path to life. It differs from 25:10 (covenant embraced inwardly), 78:7 (commandments kept as hope's fruit), and 119:2 (testimonies guarded as the mark of blessedness). The keeping turns outward to speech here, inward to fidelity elsewhere.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'guard my ways, muzzle my mouth', and the type (102) is volition — a deliberate resolve of the will. No source (103, absent): the trigger is the presence of the wicked (v.1b), but this is not coded as a source row, so the reading rests on the resolve itself. No seat (104, value 'none'): the guarding is not lodged in an organ; the mouth is muzzled but the guarding power is un-seated, a whole-self act. The bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). The operation (106) is the event of v.1: the self resolves to guard its ways so as not to sin with the tongue, keeping its mouth with a muzzle while the wicked are near — deliberate speech-restraint. The target (107) is tongue-guarding. Manner (108, value 'none'): the how is unstated, though the image of a 'muzzle' supplies the severity that the manner-row itself does not code. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent as coded rows — yet the passage's own aftermath is stark and must not be filtered (directive 6): the enforced silence does not bring peace but makes his 'distress grew worse' and his 'heart became hot within' (vv.2–3), so that the muzzle finally breaks. No effect row captures this, but the reading should note that the resolve, coded here only up to v.1, is one the psalm goes on to show failing. The coupling (112) is 'muzzle-my-mouth': the guarding is welded to the muzzle-image, a self-imposed clamp. Prohibition (113) is absent as a row, though the operation is again negatively shaped ('that I may not sin'). The discovery note (114): a self-imposed silence, the interior clamping down on speech to avoid sin. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state — an interior resolve, its arena the wicked in whose presence he will not speak.
narratives.story: A man decides he will watch every step and put a muzzle on his mouth so that he won't sin with his words — especially while wicked people are watching him. It is a deliberate, hard clamp on his own speech. But the psalm is honest about what happens next: the forced silence doesn't calm him; it makes things worse. Holding it all in, his pain grows and something burns inside until he finally has to speak. So this is a real resolve to guard the tongue, chosen freely and aimed at avoiding sin — yet the poem shows that bottling everything up can bring its own kind of trouble.
narratives.variation_note: 'guard' has two readings. Here (39:1) guarding is self-imposed speech-restraint under pressure from the wicked — a muzzle on the mouth that the psalm later shows straining and breaking. At 119:9 guarding is keeping one's way pure 'according to your word', aimed at God's word rather than at silencing the tongue. The difference is direction and outcome: a defensive clamp against sin here, a positive purity kept by the word there.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'watch / keep an eye on' (shamar — 'they watch my steps'), and the type (102) is action, not volition — an outward deed rather than an inner stance; this matters, because the same keeping-verb elsewhere in the family is a disposition, but here it is a hostile activity. No source (103, absent): the passage does not code why the enemies watch, though their malice is plain in context. No seat (104, value 'none'): the watching is not organ-located. The bearer (105) is the enemies (inferred) — and this is the point directive 5 forbids us to soften: the keeping-verb is here carried by the wicked, the descent read with the same weight as any ascent. The operation (106) is 'watch / spy on'. The target (107) is 'my steps', coded as a span-pair (from_span 280300 to_span 280301) — a real linkage in the text between the watchers and the psalmist's every movement. Manner (108) is 'lurking / in ambush' — unlike most readings this manner IS specified: the watching is predatory, done from concealment. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent as rows. The coupling (112) is a span-pair, 'paired with waiting for his life' (from 280300 to 280303): the surveillance is welded to a design on his very life — they watch his steps as they have 'waited for my life'. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): predatory surveillance; shamar here is the enemies dogging his every move, lurking to catch him — vigilance turned to a hunt for his soul. Role (115) is characteristic — read as a genuine trait of the wicked interior, not a mere qualifier. Locus (116) is external:person — the operation is lodged in the hostile persons, the arena being the psalmist they hunt; this is the inner life of the wicked expressed as watchfulness bent to harm.
narratives.story: The very same word for keeping watch shows up here on the wrong side: it is the psalmist's enemies who are watching. They track his every step, hiding and waiting like hunters in ambush, and their watching is tied to one aim — they are lying in wait for his life. This is vigilance turned into a hunt. The poem refuses to prettify it: the careful attention that can be a virtue is here the alert, patient malice of people who want to destroy him. It is a picture of what watchfulness becomes when a hostile heart puts it to use.
narratives.variation_note: 'watch' has three readings and they split sharply. Here (56:6) and at 71:10 the watchers are the enemies and the locus is external:person — predatory surveillance bent on the psalmist's life (this reading adds the 'lurking/in ambush' manner and the span-pair binding the watching to a design on his life). At 59:9 the same verb is turned around: the psalmist watches FOR God (locus external:god), the one reading in this trio that even carries a source (God as fortress). This 56:6 reading is the descent — vigilance as a hunt.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'watch / keep watch' (shamar — 'I will watch for you'), and the type (102) is action. Uniquely in this whole family, the source (103) is PRESENT (not absent): 'because God is his fortress who meets him in steadfast love' (vv.9–10), coded as a span-pair (280648→280651). This is the standout finding — nearly every other reading has no source, but here the watching is explicitly grounded: the interior keeps watch because God is its fortress. No seat (104, value 'none'): the watching is not organ-located. The bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). The operation (106) is 'watch / wait expectantly'. The target (107) is 'for God (my Strength, my fortress)', a span-pair (280648→280647) — the watching is aimed at God himself. Manner (108, value 'none'): the how is unstated. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is a span-pair, 'the refrain answered in singing' (280648→280573): the expectant watching is welded to the psalm's later song of the same words (vv.16–17), so the watching finds its resolution in praise. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the turn from the watching enemies (superscription/v.1) to the watching believer — shamar here is the psalmist keeping watch FOR God as the enemies keep watch against him, expectant waiting on his Strength and fortress. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god — the operation reaches out toward God as its arena and object.
narratives.story: In a psalm surrounded by enemies who keep watch to do harm, the psalmist takes that same watching and turns it upward: 'I will keep watch for you.' And here, unusually, the poem tells us why he can — because God is his strong fortress who comes to meet him in love. So his watching is not anxious scanning of the horizon but expectant waiting on God, confident help is coming. Even better, the very words he watches with here come back later as a song of thanks, so his waiting ends in praise. It is the bright mirror-image of the enemies' watching: the same alertness, but aimed at God and grounded in trust.
narratives.variation_note: This is the ascent among the three 'watch' readings and the only one that carries a source: the psalmist watches FOR God (locus external:god), grounded because God is his fortress, and the watching resolves into later song. It stands directly against 56:6 and 71:10, where the enemies do the watching (locus external:person) as a predatory hunt for his life. The identical verb thus swings from malice-in-ambush to trust-in-waiting — the presence of a source (a ground of confidence) is precisely what marks this reading off from the sourceless, hostile ones.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'watch / lie in wait' (shamar — 'those who watch for my life'), and the type (102) is action. No source (103, absent): the enemies' watching is ungrounded in the text — as with the other hostile reading (56:6), no cause is coded, unlike the believer's watching at 59:9 which has one. No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is the enemies (inferred). The operation (106) is 'watch / lie in wait'. The target (107) is 'for the psalmist's life', a span-pair (282046→282047) — the watching is fixed on his life itself. Manner (108) is 'consulting together' — specified, not 'none': the watchers confer, coordinating their ambush (v.10, 'consult together'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is a span-pair, 'the foes who seek his hurt' (282046→282056): the watching is welded to the wider band of enemies seeking his harm. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the enemies lying in wait, presuming God has forsaken him (v.11) — shamar here is the foes stalking the aged psalmist's life, taking his weakness as proof of abandonment, malice preying on the old. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:person — the operation is in the hostile persons, arena being the vulnerable psalmist. Directive 5 and 6: the darkest note here is that the enemies read the old man's frailty as evidence that God has abandoned him — the interior of malice interpreting weakness as a green light; this is reported without softening.
narratives.story: An old man, feeling his strength fade, is surrounded by people watching for a chance at his life. They put their heads together, plotting, lying in wait — and worst of all, they take his weakness as a sign that God has given up on him, so they close in to seize him. This is watchfulness at its cruelest: alert, patient, coordinated malice, preying on someone precisely because he is frail. The poem doesn't hide how ugly this is. It shows how a hostile heart can turn another person's vulnerability into an opportunity to strike.
narratives.variation_note: Like 56:6 this is a descent reading — the enemies do the watching (locus external:person), sourceless, aimed at the psalmist's life. It differs from 56:6 in its manner ('consulting together' rather than 'lurking/in ambush') and in its sharpest note: the foes read the aged psalmist's weakness as proof God has forsaken him. It stands opposite 59:9, where the psalmist watches FOR God in trust. The variation shows the same verb carrying coordinated malice against the weak here, expectant faith there.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep / observe' (natsar), and the type (102) is action — obedience enacted, not merely resolved. No source (103, absent) as a coded row, though the passage's flow makes the keeping the fruit of hope set on God (v.7). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is the children (inferred), the coming generation of vv.5–6 who are to be taught. The operation (106) is 'keep / obey'. The target (107) is 'his commandments'. Manner (108, value 'none'): the how is unstated. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is 'paired with hope and remembrance': the keeping is welded, in v.7, to setting hope in God and not forgetting his works — obedience held together with trust and memory as one threefold movement. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the obedience that hope in God bears as fruit. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god — the keeping is directed toward God's commandments as its object and arena; this is the generational transmission of a kept faith, obedience as the downstream fruit of taught hope.
narratives.story: This is about handing faith down the generations. The fathers are to teach the children God's mighty deeds so that when those children grow up they will do three things together: put their hope in God, remember what he has done, and keep his commandments. The obeying isn't standing on its own — it grows out of the hope and the remembering, like fruit from a root. So keeping God's commands is pictured as what naturally follows when a young heart has learned to trust and to remember. It is faith passed on, taking root, and showing up as a life that obeys.
narratives.variation_note: This 'keep' reading (78:7) is the only one that binds keeping to hope and remembrance as a threefold generational movement (coupling), aimed at commandments (locus external:god), type action. It differs from the inward covenant-embrace of 25:10, the tongue-restraint of 34:13, and the blessed-mark guarding of 119:2. Here keeping is the fruit of taught hope in the young.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep' (shamar, failed), and the type (102) is action — but a NON-action, a keeping that did not happen. No source (103, absent) as a row, though the context traces the failure to a heart 'not steadfast' and a spirit 'not faithful' (v.8). No seat (104, value 'none'): the failure is not organ-located, though v.8 names the unsteady heart as its backdrop. The bearer (105) is Ephraim / the fathers (inferred), the armed men who 'turned back on the day of battle' (v.9). The operation (106) is 'fail to keep' — the coded event is the negative: the covenant was NOT kept. The target (107) is 'God's covenant'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is 'paired with the refusal to walk in his law': the failure to keep is welded to a refusal to walk in God's law — two faces of the same rebellion. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the covenant unkept, the martial cowardice of v.9 traced to unbelief — the turning-back in battle is the outward symptom of an inward covenant-breach. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god — the (failed) keeping is oriented toward God's covenant. Directives 5–6: this is a descent read at full weight — the interior that would not keep, its unbelief surfacing as cowardice; reported without softening.
narratives.story: This is the failure of keeping. A whole tribe, armed and ready, turned and ran on the day of battle — and the psalm explains why: they did not keep God's covenant and refused to live by his law. Their cowardice on the field wasn't really about courage; it grew out of a heart that had already let go of God. Not keeping and refusing to walk in his law are two sides of the same thing. The poem lays it bare: when the inside quietly breaks faith with God, it shows up in the open as collapse when the test comes.
narratives.variation_note: Among the seven shamar 'keep' readings this is one of three failures (with 78:56 and 89:31). Here (78:10) the unkept covenant is tied to martial cowardice — unbelief surfacing as flight in battle. It contrasts with the positive keepings (103:18, 105:45, 119:17, 132:12) and even among the failures is distinct: 78:56 is treachery in the land, 89:31 the sons' neglected obedience under threat of the rod. The variation shows covenant-failure wearing different faces.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep' (shamar, negated), and the type (102) is action — again a failed keeping. No source (103, absent) as a row. No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is 'they' (inferred), the redeemed generation now settled in the land (vv.54–55). The operation (106) is 'fail to keep'. The target (107) is 'his testimonies'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent — though the passage's frame supplies the consequence (God 'full of wrath', 'utterly rejected Israel', v.59), no per-item effect is coded. The coupling (112) is 'paired with turning away treacherously': the failure to keep is welded to treacherous turning-away (v.57), like 'a deceitful bow'. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the covenant word still unheld in the land — even after redemption and settlement, the testimonies go unkept. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god. Directives 5–6: the darkness here is that the failure follows deliverance — the very people God rescued and planted still tested, rebelled, and would not keep; the ingratitude is reported plainly.
narratives.story: Even after God rescued them and gave them a homeland, the people still tested him, rebelled, and would not keep his commands. They turned away treacherously, the psalm says — like a bow that bends the wrong way and betrays the archer. The sting of it is that this comes right after all God's kindness: fed, saved, settled, and still faithless. This is keeping that fails not from hardship but from ingratitude. The poem doesn't excuse it; it shows a people who received everything and gave back rebellion.
narratives.variation_note: One of the three failure-readings of shamar 'keep'. This one (78:56) sets the unkept testimonies after redemption and settlement, coupled with treacherous turning-away ('a deceitful bow') — ingratitude as the root. It differs from 78:10 (unbelief surfacing as battlefield flight) and 89:31 (the royal sons' neglect under threat of discipline). The same failure, here framed as betrayal of a God who had already saved them.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep' (shamar, negated), and the type (102) is action — a hypothetical failure ('if they... do not keep', v.31). No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is David's children (inferred), the royal sons of the covenant. The operation (106) is 'fail to keep'. The target (107) is 'God's commandments'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent — though the passage names the consequence (punishment 'with the rod... with stripes', v.32), it is not coded as a per-item effect; and crucially God's own steadfast love is NOT withdrawn (v.33), so the failure is disciplined, not covenant-cancelling. The coupling (112) is 'paired with violating the statutes': the failure to keep is welded to the violating of statutes and forsaking of the law (vv.30–31). Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the neglected obedience of the sons. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god. This reading sits inside God's oath to David: even a keeping that fails is met not by rejection but by chastening love — a distinctive note among the failure-readings.
narratives.story: God makes a promise about David's line, and inside that promise he faces the possibility that David's descendants might fail: if they abandon his law and don't keep his commands, if they break his rules. If that happens, God says he will discipline them — with the rod, with real correction. But he immediately adds that he will not take his love away or break his own promise. So here is a failure to keep that is answered by firm love rather than rejection. It shows a God who corrects his wayward children without cutting them off.
narratives.variation_note: The third failure-reading of shamar 'keep'. Uniquely (89:31) the failure is hypothetical and set within God's oath: the sons' neglect is met with the rod yet without withdrawal of steadfast love (v.33) — disciplined, not covenant-cancelling. This differs from the accomplished failures of 78:10 (battlefield cowardice) and 78:56 (treachery after redemption). Same unkept commandments, but here held inside an unbreakable promise.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep' (shamar), and the type (102) is action — a positive keeping. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is 'those who keep covenant' (inferred), the fearers of God on whom his steadfast love rests 'from everlasting to everlasting' (v.17). The operation (106) is 'keep'. The target (107) is 'God's covenant'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is coded 'external:god' (welding the keeping to God as its object). Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the faithful who hold God's covenant, heirs of his everlasting love — the keeping marks out those on whom the enduring mercy rests. Role (115) is characteristic. The locus (116) here carries a distinctive value, 'paired with remembering to obey' — rather than the usual external:god tag, the keeping is explicitly welded to 'remember to do his commandments' (v.18): keeping and remembering-to-obey are held together as one movement. Directive 8: this locus-value is itself a finding — the passage pairs the guarding of the covenant with an active memory that issues in obedience, so that keeping is not static holding but a remembering-into-action, set against the fleeting frailty of man (v.16, 'the wind passes over it, and it is gone').
narratives.story: Against the backdrop of how quickly human life passes — here today, gone like grass in the wind — the psalm points to something that lasts: God's love rests, age after age, on those who keep his covenant. And it describes their keeping in a rich way: they keep the covenant and remember to actually do what he commands. Keeping here isn't just holding on quietly; it's a living memory that turns into obedience. These are the people who inherit God's never-ending love. Their faithfulness stands out all the brighter because everything else about human life is so brief.
narratives.variation_note: A positive shamar 'keep' reading (103:18) whose distinctive is the locus-value 'paired with remembering to obey' — keeping welded to active memory issuing in obedience, set against human frailty. It differs from the failure-readings (78:10, 78:56, 89:31) and from the other positives: 105:45 (redemption's purpose), 119:17 (keeping as life's aim), 132:12 (condition of the throne). Here keeping is a remembering-into-action by the heirs of everlasting love.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'observe' (natsar), and the type (102) is action. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is the people of God (inferred), the redeemed brought out 'with joy' and given the nations' lands (vv.43–44). The operation (106) is 'observe'. The target (107) is 'God's laws'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is coded 'external:god'. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the guarding of God's laws, the covenant's intended fruit in the redeemed. Role (115) is characteristic. The locus (116) carries the value 'paired with keeping his statutes' — this observing (natsar, of the laws) is explicitly welded to the parallel keeping (shamar, of the statutes) in the same verse. Directive 8 (preserve distinctions): v.45 holds two keeping-verbs and this reading must NOT be collapsed into its companion — natsar 'observe his laws' and shamar 'keep his statutes' stand as a deliberate poetic pair, two coded operations on one verse; the difference between them is itself the finding. Here the emphasis (natsar) is the vigilant guarding of the laws as the very purpose for which redemption was given.
narratives.story: The psalm has just retold the whole rescue — God bringing his people out of Egypt with joy and settling them in a new land — and then it names the point of it all: that they might guard his laws. All that deliverance was aimed at producing a people who watch over God's instructions and live by them. This verse actually uses two closely paired words for keeping, side by side, and this is the one that leans toward carefully guarding the laws. Freedom was given so that faithfulness could grow. The rescue was never an end in itself; it was meant to bear the fruit of a law-keeping people.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep' (shamar), and the type (102) is action. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is the people of God (inferred). The operation (106) is 'keep'. The target (107) is 'God's statutes'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is coded 'external:god'. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the purpose of the whole redemption — an obedient people, deliverance issuing in law-keeping. Role (115) is characteristic. The locus (116) carries the value 'paired with observing his laws' — this keeping (shamar, of the statutes) is welded to the parallel observing (natsar, of the laws) in the same verse. Directive 8: this reading stands beside its natsar companion (observ#1) as a deliberate pair on one line and must not be collapsed — shamar 'keep his statutes' carries the sense of holding-and-doing the statutes, while natsar 'observe his laws' carries vigilant guarding; the two verbs together frame the single purpose of the exodus. Here the shamar emphasis is the active keeping of the statutes as the intended end of God's saving acts.
narratives.story: Right after retelling how God rescued his people and gave them a land, the psalm states the goal of the whole story: that they might keep his statutes. Everything God did — the plagues, the parted sea, the wilderness provision, the gift of the land — was aimed at producing a people who would actually live by his commands. The verse uses two words for keeping side by side; this one carries the sense of holding to the statutes and doing them. So salvation had a purpose beyond escape: it was meant to create obedience. God set them free in order to make them faithful.
narratives.variation_note: This shamar 'keep' reading shares verse 105:45 with the natsar 'observe' reading (H5341:observ#1) and must be kept distinct from it (directive 8): shamar keeps 'his statutes' (holding-and-doing), natsar observes 'his laws' (vigilant guarding). Among the seven shamar 'keep' readings this one alone frames keeping as the stated purpose of the exodus/redemption, distinguishing it from the failures (78:10, 78:56, 89:31) and the other positives (103:18, 119:17, 132:12).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'observe' (shamar), and the type (102) is action. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is 'the just' (inferred), those pronounced 'blessed' in v.3. The operation (106) is 'observe / keep'. The target (107) is 'justice'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is coded 'internal:ib-state' — notably the coupling ties this observing to an inner condition, welding the outward keeping of justice to an interior state. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the keeping of justice, righteous conduct. Role (115) is characteristic. The locus (116) carries the value 'paired with the blessedness and righteousness' — the observing of justice is welded to the beatitude ('Blessed are they who observe justice, who do righteousness at all times', v.3). Directive 8: distinctively among the shamar readings, the object here is not covenant, testimonies, or word, but justice/righteous conduct — keeping turned toward right dealing itself; and its coupling is internal, marking justice-keeping as something rooted in an inner state, not merely external compliance. The passage sets this blessed keeping against v.7's fathers who 'did not remember' and 'rebelled' — the observant just over against the forgetful rebels.
narratives.story: The psalm opens with praise and then pronounces a blessing on a particular kind of person: those who keep justice and do what is right all the time. This is keeping aimed not at a rulebook but at fair, righteous dealing itself — and it flows from something settled on the inside, not just outward correctness. Such people are called blessed. And the psalm quietly contrasts them with the ancestors described a few lines later, who forgot God's kindness and rebelled. So on one side stand the steadily just; on the other, the forgetful and faithless. To keep justice, always, is held up as a truly happy way to live.
narratives.variation_note: 'observe' (shamar) has two readings. This one (106:3) is unique in aiming at 'justice' / righteous conduct (not God's word), with an internal:ib-state coupling and a locus paired with beatitude — keeping as rooted, righteous dealing. At 119:34 the same verb observes God's word, whole-heartedly, flowing from understanding (locus external:god). The difference is the object: justice itself here, the revealed word there.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'attend' (shamar), and the type (102) is action — here the keeping-verb bends toward heeding/observing with the mind. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located, though the operation is essentially mental attention. The bearer (105) is 'the wise' (inferred), the one summoned in v.43 ('Whoever is wise'). The operation (106) is 'attend to'. The target (107) is 'these things' — the whole record of God's dealings just narrated (the raising of the needy, the humbling of princes, vv.39–42). Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is coded 'internal:ib-state' — the attending is welded to an inner condition, an act of the reflective interior. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the heeding of God's dealings, wisdom's task. Role (115) is characteristic. The locus (116) carries the value 'paired with considering God's love' — the attending is welded to 'let them consider the steadfast love of the LORD' (v.43b). Directive 8: distinctively, this shamar is not keeping a law but keeping attention on God's ways — the same guarding faculty turned to contemplation; wisdom's work is to watch what God does and ponder his steadfast love. It is keeping as vigilant reflection rather than obedience.
narratives.story: At the end of a long poem about how God rescues people and reverses their fortunes, comes an invitation: if you are wise, pay careful attention to all this. Watch what God has done — how he lifts up the needy and brings down the proud — and think hard about his faithful love. Here the idea of 'keeping' turns into keeping your attention fixed, a work of the thoughtful mind. Wisdom's task is to notice God's ways and dwell on his kindness rather than let them slip by. It is less about obeying a rule and more about watching, remembering, and reflecting.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep / observe' (shamar), and the type (102) is action. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located, though the surrounding stanza names the heart as the place where the word is stored (v.11). The bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). The operation (106) is 'keep / observe'. The target (107) is 'God's word'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is 'paired with the whole KEEP-arc of the psalm' — this single keeping is welded to the vast recurring keep-theme running through Psalm 119; it is one crest of a wave that breaks again and again across the psalm (see recurrences). Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): keeping as the aim of the life God gives — 'that I may live and keep your word' (v.17); life is asked for precisely in order to keep. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god. Directive 9: this anchor gathers sixteen further occurrences of the same shamar keeping across Psalm 119 (listed in recurrences); they share this outcome — keeping God's word as the settled aim of the psalmist's whole existence — and are not re-narrated here. The distinctive of the anchor itself is that keeping is bound to the gift of life: he does not want life for its own sake but as the arena in which to keep the word.
narratives.story: In this great psalm about loving God's instructions, the writer prays a striking prayer: 'Deal well with me so that I may live — and keep your word.' He doesn't want life just to have it; he wants life in order to obey. Keeping God's word is the very point of his existence. This desire runs like a heartbeat through the whole psalm, surfacing again and again in verse after verse. Here, at one of its clearest moments, living and keeping are tied together — as if to be alive is simply to be given more room to hold on to what God has said.
narratives.variation_note: This shamar 'keep' anchor (119:17) leads the largest recurrence-set in the family (sixteen further verses of Psalm 119) and its distinctive is binding keeping to the gift of life ('that I may live and keep'). Among the seven shamar keepings it differs from the failures (78:10, 78:56, 89:31), from 103:18 (remembering-into-action), 105:45 (redemption's purpose), and 132:12 (the throne's condition): here keeping is the very aim for which life is sought.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep / guard' (natsar), and the type (102) is action. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located, though the same verse names the 'whole heart' with which the blessed seek God (v.2b). The bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred), standing for all 'those who keep his testimonies'. The operation (106) is 'keep / guard'. The target (107) is 'God's testimonies'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is 'paired with the whole KEEP-arc of the psalm'. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the guarding of the testimonies that marks the blessed — 'Blessed are those who keep his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart' (v.2). Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god. Directive 9: this natsar anchor gathers seven further occurrences across Psalm 119 (recurrences); they share the outcome of blessed, whole-hearted guarding of the testimonies and are not re-narrated. Directive 8: note the distinction from the shamar keeping in the same stanza (119:17, keep#6) — natsar here is the guarding/watching-over of the testimonies that opens the psalm's beatitude, welded to whole-hearted seeking, whereas the shamar keeping is bound to the gift of life; the two keeping-verbs run in parallel through Psalm 119 and their difference is a finding.
narratives.story: Right at the start of this long psalm comes a blessing: happy are the people who guard God's words and seek him with their whole heart. To keep his testimonies here means to watch over them, treasure them, hold them close — and it goes hand in hand with wanting God completely, not half-heartedly. This is the mark of the truly blessed life. The idea returns many times through the psalm in the same key. Guarding God's word and seeking God wholeheartedly are shown to be two parts of one devoted life.
narratives.variation_note: 'keep' (natsar) has four readings. This 119:2 anchor is the whole-hearted guarding of the testimonies that marks the blessed, leading a seven-verse recurrence-set in Psalm 119; it runs parallel to (yet distinct from) the shamar keeping of the same psalm (119:17). It differs from 25:10 (covenant embraced inwardly as the ground for seeing God's ways as love), 34:13 (tongue-restraint), and 78:7 (commandments kept as hope's generational fruit). The object here is the testimonies, coupled to whole-hearted seeking.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep / observe' (shamar), and the type (102) is action. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred), voiced through the 'young man' of v.9. The operation (106) is 'keep / observe'. The target (107) is 'God's word'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is 'paired with the whole KEEP-arc of the psalm'. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): keeping the way pure by the word — 'How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word' (v.9). Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god. Directive 8 and 10: this shamar 'guard' asks and answers a question — purity of life is achieved by guarding one's way 'according to your word'; the guarding here is instrumental and self-directed (guarding one's own way/conduct), yet its measure is God's word. It differs from the family's other 'guard' (39:1), where guarding was a defensive muzzle on the tongue under the eye of the wicked; here guarding is the positive means to a pure path, the word supplying the standard by which the young life is kept clean.
narratives.story: The psalm asks a very practical question: how can a young person keep their life clean? And it answers plainly: by guarding it according to God's word. Purity isn't left to chance or willpower alone — it comes from watching over your own way and measuring it against what God has said. So the guarding is aimed at one's own conduct, but the rule for it is God's instruction. It is a hopeful answer to a real problem, pointing a young life toward the word as its guardrail.
narratives.variation_note: 'guard' has two readings. This one (119:9) is positive and instrumental — guarding one's own way pure 'according to your word', the word as the standard, aimed at God's word (locus external:god). It contrasts with 39:1, a defensive self-muzzling of the tongue before the wicked that the psalm shows straining and breaking. The difference: purity kept by the word here, sin averted by forced silence there.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep / guard' (natsar), and the type (102) is action — here in the completed/past aspect ('I have kept'). No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located, though the stanza is full of interior language ('My soul is consumed with longing', v.20). The bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). The operation (106) is 'keep / guard'. The target (107) is 'God's testimonies'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is 'paired with the whole KEEP-arc of the psalm'. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): keeping pleaded as ground for relief from scorn — 'Take away from me scorn and contempt, for I have kept your testimonies' (v.22). Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god. Directive 10: what distinguishes this reading is its function within a prayer — the past-tense keeping is offered as the basis of an appeal: because he has guarded God's testimonies, he asks to be freed from the scorn and contempt heaped on him (with princes plotting against him, v.23). Keeping here is not merely described but pleaded; the faithful record of guarding becomes the ground on which the sufferer asks for vindication. This anchor also gathers one recurrence (119:56).
narratives.story: Surrounded by scorn and with powerful people plotting against him, the psalmist prays for relief — and the reason he offers is this: 'I have kept your words.' He has guarded and held on to God's instructions, and now he lays that faithfulness before God as the basis of his appeal: take this contempt away from me, because I have been true to you. Here keeping isn't just something he does; it becomes his plea. His track record of holding fast to God's word is what he leans on when he asks to be defended. Faithfulness becomes the ground of the prayer.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'set' (shavah — 'I set your rules before me'), and the type (102) is action. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). The operation (106) is 'set the rules before oneself'. The target (107) is 'God's word'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' — welded to the wider setting/choosing theme. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the deliberate setting of God's rules before the eyes — 'I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me' (v.30). Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god. Directive 10: this 'set' pairs a chosen way ('I have chosen the way of faithfulness') with a fixed gaze ('I set your rules before me') — choice and continual attention held together. It stands beside the family's other 'set' (16:8) but differs pointedly: there the object set before the self was the LORD himself (locus internal:ib-state, God-before-me); here the object is God's rules/word (locus external:god). The same deliberate act of placing-before-oneself is aimed once at a Person to be gazed upon and once at a rule to be lived by — a real shift in object that the variation makes visible.
narratives.story: The psalmist tells us he has made a choice — the way of faithfulness — and then describes how he keeps to it: 'I set your rules before me.' He deliberately keeps God's instructions in front of his eyes, like a traveler keeping a map always open. Choosing the right road and keeping it constantly in view go together. It is an act of the will, freely made and steadily maintained. To decide on faithfulness and then to keep God's word always before you is how the good way is actually walked.
narratives.variation_note: 'set' has two readings. Here (119:30) the object set before the self is God's rules/word (locus external:god), paired with the chosen 'way of faithfulness'. At 16:8 the object was the LORD himself held before the inner eye (locus internal:ib-state), issuing in unshakable steadiness. The same deliberate placing-before-oneself is aimed once at a rule to live by and once at a Person to gaze on — the shift in object is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep / observe' (shamar), and the type (102) is action. No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located, though the verse names the 'whole heart' as the manner of the keeping ('observe it with my whole heart'). The bearer (105) is the psalmist (inferred). The operation (106) is 'keep / observe'. The target (107) is 'God's word' (the law). Manner (108, value 'none') is coded, yet the text itself supplies 'with my whole heart' — the manner-row is empty while the verse names a whole-hearted manner, a place where the coding's silence and the text diverge and the text should be honoured. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent. The coupling (112) is 'paired with the whole KEEP-arc of the psalm'. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): keeping that flows from understanding, whole-hearted — 'Give me understanding, that I may keep your law and observe it with my whole heart' (v.34). Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god. Directive 10: the distinctive of this observing is its dependence on a prior gift — the psalmist prays for understanding as the enabling condition of keeping ('Give me understanding, THAT I may keep'); obedience is sought as the fruit of an illumined mind and pledged with the whole heart. This anchor gathers one recurrence (119:146).
narratives.story: The psalmist prays for understanding — but notice what he wants it for: 'give me understanding, so that I may keep your law and obey it with all my heart.' He isn't after knowledge for its own sake; he wants to grasp God's instruction precisely so he can live it out completely. Real obedience, he knows, grows from real understanding, and he means to give it everything, holding nothing back. So he asks God to open his mind as the first step toward a whole-hearted, faithful life. Understanding and obeying are linked — one feeds the other.
narratives.variation_note: 'observe' (shamar) has two readings. This one (119:34) observes God's law/word, flowing from a prayed-for understanding and pledged with the whole heart (locus external:god), and leads a recurrence at 119:146. It differs from 106:3, where the same verb keeps 'justice' / righteous conduct itself (locus internal:ib-state, coupled to beatitude). The object shifts from the revealed word here to justice there, and the ground shifts from illumined understanding to inner righteousness.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'keep' (shamar), and the type (102) is action — here conditional ('If your sons keep...'). No source (103, absent). No seat (104, value 'none'): not organ-located. The bearer (105) is David's sons (inferred). The operation (106) is 'keep'. The target (107) is 'God's covenant'. Manner (108, value 'none'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent — though the passage attaches an outcome (their sons 'shall sit on your throne forever'), it is coded not as an effect but as the locus-pairing. The coupling (112) is coded 'external:god'. Prohibition (113) is absent. The discovery note (114): the sons' keeping, the condition on which the enduring throne hangs — 'If your sons keep my covenant and my testimonies... their sons also forever shall sit on your throne' (v.12). Role (115) is characteristic. The locus (116) carries the value 'paired with the throne promised' — the keeping is welded to the dynastic promise; here alone in the family the keeping is the hinge of a covenant with the house of David, its reward the enduring throne. Directive 10: this reading turns keeping into a condition — not a description of what is or a lament over what failed, but the 'if' on which a promise pivots; the interior fidelity of the sons is the load-bearing term of a royal covenant.
narratives.story: God has sworn a promise to David about his royal line, and here it comes with a condition attached: if David's sons keep God's covenant and the terms he teaches them, then their descendants will sit on the throne forever. Everything hangs on that little word 'if.' The keeping of faith by one generation opens the door to the next. It is a promise and a responsibility bound together — the enduring dynasty depends on the sons staying true. Faithfulness here isn't just admired; it is the hinge on which the whole future turns.
narratives.variation_note: Among the seven shamar 'keep' readings this one (132:12) alone makes keeping the condition of a dynastic promise (locus 'paired with the throne promised') — an 'if' on which the enduring Davidic throne pivots. It differs from the failures (78:10, 78:56, 89:31), from 103:18 (remembering-into-action), 105:45 (redemption's purpose), and 119:17 (keeping as life's aim). Here keeping is the load-bearing term of a royal covenant.
